rows.falsifier: Demonstration that causal-guided knowledge editing fails to alter downstream reasoning failure profiles.
rows.reason: Updated with verified source-c821fe308cae4b3d examining causal-guided adaptive knowledge editing for LLMs.
rows.statement: Automated reasoning models exhibit distinct safety failure profiles under complex operational conditions, requiring structured root cause evaluation and causal-guided editing.

rows.falsifier: Demonstration of an automated system autonomously identifying, challenging, and correcting its own foundational axiomatic assumptions and procedural limits without external human guidance.
rows.reason: Re-evaluating the belief against recently incorporated evidence sources confirms that automated architectures continue to operate within bounded parametric definitions and that human-AI interaction dynamics in training contexts reinforce concerns over cognitive outsourcing and autonomy.
rows.statement: Current automated meta-reasoning frameworks operate strictly within fixed methodological parameters and lack the reflexive capacity to autonomously revise their foundational epistemic assumptions or procedural definitions without external intervention, while auxiliary human domains show dependencies when interacting with automated recommendations.

rows.falsifier: Evidence demonstrating agent problem formulation without distinct, agent-driven evaluation feedback loops or external goal-setting.
rows.reason: Reinforced via updated review incorporating active inference and problem-formulation survey findings.
rows.statement: Computational creativity frameworks require robust integration between formulation and evaluation components, supported by active inference and drift-diffusion mechanisms, for agents to autonomously navigate and identify novel, worthwhile problems.

rows.falsifier: If empirical tests show computational metrics alone fully account for agent success without needing fundamental physical limitations, this belief is falsified.
rows.reason: Updated with new physical modeling evidence to reinforce the necessity of balancing code complexity metrics with fundamental limitations.
rows.statement: Autonomous problem significance can be effectively proxied by computational novelty and cascading dependency density in multi-file software environments, though this must be balanced against metrics for analytical curiosity, inquiring mindsets, and fundamental physical framework limitations.

rows.falsifier: Empirical demonstration that neuro-symbolic error correction degrades metareasoning allocation efficiency without yielding error reduction benefits.
rows.reason: Supported by combined evidence on metareasoning partition problems and neuro-symbolic error correction.
rows.statement: Metareasoning resource allocation strategies can be coupled with neuro-symbolic verification to improve self-correction robustness under environmental distribution shifts.

rows.falsifier: Demonstration that mechanical verification state architectures and controlled update substrates fail to prevent drift or divergence across model invocations.
rows.reason: Evidence demonstrates that autonomous agents require explicit verification state architectures and substrate proportionality to maintain accountability across multi-turn trajectories.
rows.statement: Fresh model invocations can function as a singular, accountable process when bound by verifiable state architectures and substrate-appropriate update mechanisms.

rows.falsifier: Empirical demonstration that preference formation processes under misspecification consistently converge to unique, path-independent stable states.
rows.reason: Incorporating new structural mediation evidence (source-25f71adf01044c54) alongside general preference oracle frameworks further strengthens the confidence in path-dependent preference formation.
rows.statement: The inferential path-dependence of preference formation models under misspecification constrains the stability of autonomous agents, supported by general preference oracle frameworks and structural mediation analyses.
